group.passage: City dwellers today expect to find a park within walking distance, and few ask who pays for it. Yet the idea that a government should buy land, shape it into a landscape and open it to everyone free of charge is less than two hundred years old. It grew out of the crowded industrial towns of nineteenth-century Britain. One of those towns was Birkenhead, across the river from Liverpool. Its population jumped from about 200 in 1821 to over 24,000 by 1851, and a committee of Parliament had already warned that fast-growing towns were harming the health of the poor. In 1843, an act of Parliament allowed Birkenhead to borrow money to buy land for a public park. The designer, Joseph Paxton, set aside plots around the edges for large houses, and selling these plots helped pay for the project. When the park opened in 1847, a crowd of about 10,000 came to celebrate. Other parks of the time had mostly been gifts from wealthy donors or charged their visitors. Birkenhead Park, by contrast, belonged to the public and was open free to anyone, whatever their class. This was what most impressed a young American named Frederick Law Olmsted, who visited the park in 1850 while touring England on foot. He called it a "people's garden" and later wrote that the poorest farm worker in Britain could enjoy every corner of it as freely as the queen. Back home, New York was growing fast, and for many residents the only green spaces nearby were cemeteries. In 1853, the state approved a large park in the middle of Manhattan, on rocky, swampy land that builders had no use for. A design contest in 1858 drew 33 entries, and the winner was the Greensward Plan by Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux. Its roads were sunk below ground level, so carriages could cross the park without disturbing people on foot. Covering about 843 acres, Central Park is more than six times the size of the park that inspired it. Yet both rest on the same belief: in a crowded city, green space should belong to everyone, not just to those who can afford it.

translation_zh.text:
綠地屬於每一個人：公共公園的誕生

今天住在城市裡的人，都期待走路就能到一座公園，卻很少有人問是誰出錢的。然而，「由政府買下土地、把它造成一片風景，再免費開放給所有人」這個想法，歷史還不到兩百年。它誕生於十九世紀英國擁擠的工業城鎮。

伯肯黑德（Birkenhead）就是這樣的一個城鎮，和利物浦隔河相望。它的人口從 1821 年的大約 200 人，暴增到 1851 年的兩萬四千多人；而英國國會的一個委員會早已警告，快速成長的城鎮正在損害窮人的健康。1843 年，一項國會法案允許伯肯黑德借錢買地，興建一座公共公園。設計師約瑟夫‧帕克斯頓（Joseph Paxton）在公園四周留下土地蓋大房子，賣掉這些土地的錢則用來支付工程費用。1847 年公園開幕時，大約有一萬人前來慶祝。當時其他的公園大多是富人捐贈的，或是要向遊客收費；相較之下，伯肯黑德公園屬於大眾，不論身分階級，任何人都可以免費進入。

這一點最讓一位名叫斐德列克‧洛‧歐姆斯德（Frederick Law Olmsted）的年輕美國人印象深刻。他在 1850 年徒步旅行英格蘭時參觀了這座公園。他稱它為「人民的花園」，後來還寫道，英國最窮的農場工人也能像女王一樣，自由地享受公園的每一個角落。

回到美國，紐約正在快速成長，對許多居民來說，附近唯一的綠地就是墓地。1853 年，州政府核准在曼哈頓中央興建一座大型公園，用地是一片多石、多沼澤、建商根本用不上的土地。1858 年的設計競圖吸引了 33 件作品，獲勝的是歐姆斯德和建築師卡爾弗特‧沃克斯（Calvert Vaux）的「綠草地計畫」（Greensward Plan）。這個設計把穿越公園的道路下沉到地面以下，讓馬車可以穿過公園，又不會打擾步行的人。

中央公園占地約 843 英畝，是啟發它的那座公園的六倍多。然而兩者都建立在同一個信念上：在擁擠的城市裡，綠地應該屬於每一個人，而不只屬於負擔得起的人。
